   - His insight is correct: raising keep (growing the tail) re-expands messages that were summarized (and no longer exist) — you can't uninform what you've forgotten. If the agent then wants to grow the tail back into the summarized region, those messages come back into context as raw — the agent can re-read them. So it's not uninformed in the sense that the content is lost (the DB has it), but the agent can't make an informed choice about which range to grow to without first reading (reporting) the content of the region — a report round-trip. | **timing** | when should I start compacting? | nudge bands (your #4) |
| **informed choice** | what would I keep, and what's dropped? | your informed-default idea + the Part 3 report forms |

The interactions that matter: the **nudge line's text should point at the recommendation** (not just "self-compact now"); the **self-marker needs the recommendation** for an informed boundary; and the **adaptive keep becomes redundant** once informed choice exists (it only retains value for the auto-at-cap case, where the agent can't act).

## 2. Per-proposal feedback

**keep-N surface (your #2).**
- `keepMessages` rename: agreed — it's a message count driving the same semantics as compact_memory's, not a token budget.
- Your Part 3 forms: all four are good. Numbered rows with internal messageID mapping = yes (the agent never types dense ids — this also kills the Pattern-4 dense-numeric failure mode); tool-target detail = the report already carries it (read filePath / bash command / webfetch url) — the token-efficient form keeps that, drops content echoes; `last: N` = yes; "last N as info for the next compaction" = exactly your informed-default idea (see below).
- Your downside insight is **right and sharper than mine**: shrinking is informed (you know the boundary); growing re-includes raw messages you no longer remember — though nothing is lost (the DB keeps them, the report restores the knowledge). So the surface is primarily a **shrink lever** (the emergency-keep=18 fix case); growing stays available but documented as "you are re-reading what you no longer remember."
- `keepMessages=0`: at dispatch it **already exists** (the 25.8k floor = the summary alone). On the tail surface keep=0 must stay rejected by the floor-6 — a zero raw tail breaks the post-compaction protocol (the re-read head files are the resume basis). And "drop everything before the last compaction" already works as the next compaction with a small keep — each new summary re-covers the whole session head (the old summary gets re-summarized into it).

**usage-adaptive keep (your #1).**
- "Does it clash with keep-N?" — no: precedence, not clash. Explicit agent keep always wins; the adaptive formula would only apply when nothing is specified (the auto-at-cap / emergency / forgotten-keep cases).
- But your follow-through is the right question: with the **informed default** (below) and the **self-marker**, the blind adaptive cap loses most of its value — an agent choosing from a content-based recommendation beats a formula. Its residual value is only the auto-at-cap case (static 30/40k is "good enough" there). **My recommendation: park it** — revisit if auto-at-cap keeps ever prove bad in practice. This answers "why is this needed?" with "it isn't, given your two newer ideas."

**gauge-nudge-bands (your #4).**
- Given live 0.85, a new 0.80 rung is marginal (5 points earlier). The real improvement is the **line text**: today's "self-compact now" contradicts the stop-line triage — at 85 % the correct action is *estimate the calls left; compact only if the unit won't fit*. Reframe the proposal: **triage text on the existing 0.85 line** (optionally + a config-gated 0.80 early rung), and once the recommendation leg exists, the line can point at it ("run the context_trim recommendation, then compact with the keep you choose"). Effort stays S; or defer entirely if you're satisfied with the current line.

## 3. Your BIG QUESTION — can we set our own compaction marker?

**Yes — mechanically feasible, and I verified the schema, not just the concept:**

- The window is re-derived **from the DB at every step** (plan36 research; `context_trim tail` is live-accepted zero-restart) — so your "trigger a restart" step is probably unnecessary.
- The marker **quartet** is fully known (the host guard at message-v2.ts:568, mirrored in our own `context_trim.ts`): a **user row** whose parts carry `{ type: "compaction", tail_start_id: <existing message id> }` + the **first assistant row strictly after it** with `info.summary` (+ summary text). Guard: `tailIndex < compactionIndex && summaryIndex > compactionIndex` — fail → full history. All four elements are writable with the same sqlite access `context_trim tail` already uses for its in-place `tail_start_id` write; plan36 explicitly named "creating a marker" as the remaining option.
- So your idea 1 becomes: at ~90 % (nudge) the agent **writes the summary itself** (same model the host dispatch would use — but at the agent's chosen moment, with full context, compaction-style — we have the original prompt), then a tool call writes the quartet (summary + marker + `tail_start_id` at the chosen boundary), and the next step's window = summary + chosen tail.
- The design decision this forces: **route it through `compact_memory` as a new mode/arg** (agent-supplied summary + boundary) rather than raw DB writes — so the protocol machinery runs: budget increment + ctx.log COMPACT line + the two-artifact dump + queued-message relay. And it should **consume one budget compaction** — it is a compaction (wall-time cost, trims the window, reclaims speed); unbudgeted self-markers would let the agent loop to the wall and break the pacing.
- Your idea 2 (selective/multi-marker keep): your infeasibility conclusion is **confirmed** — the window is always the LATEST marker's summary + one contiguous slice `tailIndex..compactionIndex` (host `findLastIndex`); older markers stay in the DB but are dead once a newer marker exists. Non-contiguous retention is structurally impossible with this mechanism.

## 4. Developed build order (proposal)

1. **keep-N surface, `keepMessages` naming** (approved; S) — ships first, independent.
2. **context_trim recommendation leg** (your Part 3 + your informed default; M): a token-efficient report form — numbered rows, tool-target detail only, `last: N` — plus a short **recommendation block: 2–3 boundary options anchored at messageIDs** (stable across your pre/post-compaction deliberation, exactly your "starting points don't shift" point) with mass breakdowns ("keep from msg 214: retain ≈42k — read 20k / thought 15k / shell 7k; drop ≈90k") + the oldest-kept message's one-line content hint.
3. **self-marker mode on `compact_memory`** (M–L): agent summary + boundary → quartet write + full protocol (budget/ctx.log/dump/relay). Acceptance: fixture-DB smoke (write quartet, verify the guard passes + window re-derivation) + one live throwaway-session test.
4. **nudge line reframe** (S, after #2 so the line can reference the recommendation).
5. **adaptive keep: parked.**

## Open questions (ordered)

1. **Self-marker**: confirm the two load-bearing choices — (a) it consumes one budget compaction, (b) the summary is written by the agent (current model, compaction-style), not dispatched through the host's summarize endpoint.
2. **Nudge line**: triage text on the existing 0.85 line, a new 0.80 early rung, both, or defer (you've seen no problems)?
3. **Recommendation shape**: 2–3 messageID-anchored options + read/thought/shell mass split + oldest-kept hint — does that match your sketch ("50k read, 30k thought, 20k shell, oldest retained message detail"), or do you want the options presented differently (e.g., as keepMessages counts instead of ids)?

Once you rule, I revise the three proposal files (or collapse them into one package proposal with the parked item noted) and re-file for decision.

Verified the mechanics first — the regrouping decision rests on one fact, so here it is up front.

## 1. What plan36 §5 actually allows (the unit-3 mechanics, measured)

Selective drop is **viable, and covers exactly the "current context" case you describe**:

- **Safe zone** (the only deletions that can't break a live session): complete finished turns (user row + its assistant row(s)) strictly before the current last user message, and outside the marker quartet — i.e. **both** in the pre-marker retained tail ("those shrink the retained tail — that is the intended trim") **and** in the post-marker current context; plus per-part deletion of individual call/result pairs from OLD assistant rows (call + result cohabit one row, so a pair deletes cleanly, no dangling references).
- **Not viable**: the current last turn (deleting it re-runs an old turn — the active prompt swaps), the marker quartet (full-history degeneration), part-only deletion of the current turn.
- **Destructive**: deleting a message row cascade-deletes its parts (no orphans) — so reversibility needs a design element: **tombstone the deleted rows (archive them to a JSON file) before the delete**, else they're gone.
- One terminology note: the *original* "Unit 3" in the context_trim proposal was the **non-destructive per-message toggle fork** (your learning fork). What you're describing now is plan36's **row-deletion channel** (destructive selective drop). I'll build what you're describing; the toggle fork stays parked as it was.

## 2. Investment: marker-compaction vs. unit-3 — regroup around unit 3, yes

Your "replaces it anyway" is right **for the mid-window cases**: with selective drop, most compactions become unnecessary — you drop the heavy finished turns / big reads / webfetches, keep everything else raw (including the session start), no summary, no backend prefill, no RAM checkpoint. Marker-compaction's claims survive exactly one slot: **the cap backstop** — when the window is full and dropping the heavies can't free enough (many medium-weight messages), a summary is still the efficient move. But that backstop is not urgent to build: the vanilla host compaction stays as the cap path in the meantime.

So: **yes — regroup the package around unit 3, and demote the marker-compaction to the "cap backstop" slot** (build after unit 3, or earlier only if the cap case bites first). The collected ideas all carry over:

| unit | piece | effort |
|---|---|---|
| **U0** | keep-N surface, `keepMessages` naming (already approved) — the shrink lever | S |
| **U1** | the recommendation leg (your "cut down report"): numbered rows, tool-target detail only, `last: N`, **3 anchored options — low / medium / high retention — each with the read/thought/shell mass split + oldest-kept hint**, messageID-anchored so deliberation doesn't shift the boundary | M |
| **U2** | **unit 3 selective drop**: per-turn + per-call/result-pair deletion, safe-zone validation (mirror the guard fail-closed), tombstone archive, live-DB write coordination (proven by the landed `tail`) | M–L |
| **U3** | marker-compaction (the cap backstop): agent-written summary + quartet write via a `compact_memory` mode, full protocol (budget / ctx.log / dump), consumes one budget compaction | S–M |
| **U4** | nudge policy reframe (below) | S |
| parked | adaptive-keep (revisit if auto-at-cap keeps prove bad) | — |

U1 and U2 share infrastructure (the per-message mass data feeds both the retention options **and** the "biggest droppable" list for U2 — I'd add to the recommendation leg: a top-N heavy finished turns / call-results list with turn number + mass, so U2's targets come from the same cheap read).

## 3. Your compact_trim / resume observation

- **A trim needs no resume message** — by construction. `context_trim` is mid-session, zero-resume: the context re-derives from the DB at the next step and the session continues unbroken. There is no "compacted/trimmed session resume" event to deliver into.
- **Unit 4 of auto_resume stays** — its revival branch is the recovery mechanism (a dead session coming back; the cap case still needs it). What changes: the queued-message relay (`compact_memory.message`) shrinks in importance — for mid-session trims and marker-compactions there's nothing to relay mid-session (the queued message is delivered on a *later revival*, queued-relay semantics only; no host `promptAsync` exists on our paths). So "resume on usage" as an active feature: effectively obsolete, as you observe — keep the machinery, expect rare use.
- The unit-naming collision (auto_resume units vs. context_trim units vs. the auto-resume proposal's units — all "Unit N" for different things) — noted, NAP-only; candidate for the next docs pass.

## 4. "Replace the prompt budget triggers via nudges?"

Mostly yes — and it's the strongest simplification in the set:

- **Move**: the static 80/90/95 ladders (currently prompt text) become the live plugin nudge — config-driven thresholds, live-measured ratio, and the **informed recommendation one-liner on the triage rung** ("triage line: calls left in unit won't fit — options: keep from msg 214 ≈42k | msg 180 ≈68k | msg 120 ≈120k; or drop turn 14 (≈18k read)").
- **Keep in prompt**: only the *semantics* (what each rung means to do: estimate → stop at checkpoint → compact with chosen keep / drop the heavies) as fallback for sessions where the nudge is suppressed (Direct sessions get no nudge — verified gate) and for the pre-nudge zone.
- Result: one source of truth for budget policy (config), no prompt-memory dependence near the stop line (the exact failure mode the band proposal targeted), and the 0.80 rung you asked for falls out for free (it's the triage rung, in line with the prompt's existing 80 % rule).

## Open questions (ordered)

1. **Terminology + scope**: confirm I build the *destructive drop channel* (safe-zone + tombstone) as the new "unit 3", with the original non-destructive toggle fork staying parked?
2. **Reversibility**: tombstone archive before delete (deleted turns → JSON archive in the loop folder or `.opencode/temp/`, referenceable by the report) — GO?
3. **Nudge policy**: confirm "mostly replace the prompt ladders, keep them as fallback for Direct/suppressed sessions" + the 0.80 triage rung with the recommendation one-liner — and one config key per rung vs. one threshold list in `compact_budget.json`?

If you rule, I collapse the three commented proposals into one package proposal (U0–U4, adaptive-keep parked, marker-compaction in the backstop slot) and re-file it for decision.

Short answer to three questions:

1. Is storing the filter in the DB (an additional field/parameter on session messages, e.g. active/included) the canonical way?
2. Does that count as destructive?
3. How does vanilla (mainline) opencode react to added DB fields it doesn't expect — ignored, or never read?

Short answer based on the facts I've measured:

1. DB is canonical — yes, the DB is the single source of truth for the prompt (plan36: context is re-derived from the DB every step. A file-based filter would also work because the fork reads files, but the DB is the canonical location, and it survives session retrieval/porting). Caveat: if stored as a column, you need to modify the fork's DB schema — that's heavier. Better approach: store it inside an existing JSON blob (the `data` column of message/part — sql.ts:77,92 — "message/part metadata is in a JSON blob (`data` column)"). So: not a new column, but a small JSON field (e.g. `data.included: false` / `data.filter: "off"`) inside the existing message row's `data` blob — zero schema change. The fork's assembly reads `data.included` (skip if false). This is what he's calling an "extra field/parameter for active/included."

2. Destructive? No — it's a non-destructive metadata annotation (a JSON edit to an existing row, adding a field — the message content is not modified/deleted). By his own line: destructive = row/data deletion. An added field = additive metadata. (The context_trim tail precedent is already an in-place JSON edit of a part row — same class, and he's already approved that as live.)

3. Vanilla opencode's reaction: the message/part metadata lives in a JSON `data` blob. The mainline code reads specific keys from it, and unknown extra keys are ignored (JSON is read by key access, not by schema validation — sql.ts stores/returns the whole blob, and the code destructures known fields). It's never validated, so no error. It just exists in the blob. (Also: mainline doesn't call our fork's filter logic at all — the field is simply inert data to it.)

Caveats to include (short but honest):
- The field needs to go on the message row's `data` (or the part's data) — a JSON edit to an existing row. The mainline host itself never writes/reads it → it's inert on mainline.
- One practical caveat: if the mainline ever rewrites/normalizes that data blob (e.g. some updatePart that rebuilds the object), an unknown field could get dropped — unknown fields are ignored on read, but if the host rebuilds the object with only known fields, the annotation gets lost. From what I've measured: `updatePart` spreads (`{...part, ...changes}`) — it preserves extra fields. But I shouldn't over-claim. The short answer is: ignored on read (key access, no schema validation), inert on mainline. Rebuilds via spread preserve it.

Short answers:

1. **Yes, the DB is the canonical spot** — and you can do it without a schema change: message/part metadata lives in JSON `data` blobs (`sql.ts:77,92`), so the filter is a **small JSON field on the existing message row** (`data.included: false` or similar) — no new column, no table. The fork's assembly reads it per step (context is re-derived from the DB every step, so it works for retrieved sessions too — exactly the durability a file wouldn't have).

2. **No, it doesn't count as destructive** — it's an additive metadata annotation (a JSON edit of an existing row; no message data touched or deleted). Same class as the already live-accepted `context_trim tail` (which edits one JSON field on a part row in place).

3. **Mainline ignores it** — the host reads `data` by key access, never schema-validates the blob, so an unknown extra field is simply never read and never errors. It's inert data on mainline (the filter logic is fork-only code that mainline never calls). One caveat: fields survive host rewrites only if the host spreads the object (`{...part, ...changes}` — which `updatePart` does); if mainline ever rebuilt a blob from scratch, the annotation would drop silently — worth a pin in the fork smoke, not a blocker.
